unit.title: Teaching embedded and IoT systems at university

video.title: Designing an IoT capstone: Labs, safety and rubrics
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Prof Farah - head of department, Amman
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

scenes.narration: Last year our department bought forty development kits and set a capstone in week one. By week six, half the teams were still debugging their first blinking light.
Today: how to sequence hardware labs into a capstone, keep them safe and affordable, and assess teams fairly with a rubric.
Scaffolding means structured support that is removed step by step. Early labs give working code and one change to make. Later labs give a goal and a parts list. The capstone gives only a problem.
One proven sequence: digital input and output, then sensors and the converter, then timers and interrupts, then low power, then networking. Each lab produces a part the capstone will reuse.
Here is a fourteen-week split that worked: eight weeks of scaffolded labs, a week to propose, and five weeks of capstone with a midpoint demo.
Keep labs at low voltage, and keep lithium cells charged only on proper chargers. Simulators let students test code before touching hardware, and shared kits with a checkout log keep costs down.

A working demo can hide luck. Assess the engineering too: a requirements list, a measured power budget, a test log, and an individual reflection. Peer assessment helps spread marks fairly inside a team.
Quick check! Why did half our teams stall in the first six weeks?
They faced an open problem before they had the basic skills. The kits were fine. A scaffolded sequence of labs would have built those skills first.
In the app, open the board lab. Run “Night light” on a virtual board, change its code, and run it again before anyone touches real hardware.
Your turn. In a team of four, one student did almost nothing. Which evidence best supports adjusting individual marks?
Structured peer assessment with the commit and test logs. Remember: scaffold before the capstone, keep labs safe and cheap, and assess the engineering as well as the demo.
Try it this term: list the skills your capstone needs. Then check that an earlier lab teaches each one, and add a lab for any skill that is missing.

checkpoints.prompt: Why did half the teams stall in the first six weeks?

options.text: An open problem came before basic skills

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: scaffolded labs should build the skills before the open capstone.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the kits worked; the students lacked the skills an earlier lab sequence would have built.

checkpoints.prompt: One of four teammates did almost nothing. Best evidence for adjusting marks?

options.text: Structured peer assessment plus commit and test logs

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: several independent records of contribution are fairer than one impression.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the demo shows the team's result, not who contributed; peer ratings and logs do.
